component-design.decision: The component decomposition, responsibilities and flows (capture -> detect -> correct -> feedback), co-designed

requirements-nfr.decision: Latency budgets (<10ms dictionary, <500ms LLM), accuracy bar and false-positive tolerance, resource footprint

ui-ux.decision: Overlay bubble behavior, the two-tier sound design, undo/dismiss of a correction, tray interactions

agenda: Which design method / decomposition vocabulary governs the structure?
Which process topology: single tray-app process, two-process split, or app + service?
Which hook isolation strategy: managed P/Invoke, native C++ DLL, or managed-first swap-ready?
Which threading/pipeline model keeps the input hook non-blocking?
Which volatilities are isolated, where does state live, and what is out of scope this iteration?
architecture-core.decision: Strict IDesign (role call-rules as binding law, enforced by CI architecture test): accessors call no system component and publish outward; engines own algorithms, call no engines/managers, return via callback; managers own flow, call engines and accessors only. Single tray-app process. Managed WH_KEYBOARD_LL hook on a dedicated thread, native-swap-ready behind the keystroke accessor contract (swap triggers: callback-latency violations or field AV false-positives). .NET Channel<T> pipeline with a single serialized correction executor owning the race-safety journal and self-injection suppression. LLM detection is an accessor (external world), dictionary detection an engine. State: WordAssemblyEngine holds the current word; TranscriptEngine owns the rolling multi-word journal (suspect-span widening, trailing remap applied twice, correction transactions, epoch after layout switch); manager holds only flow state and commands the privacy wipe. Out of scope: Windows Service, IME languages, dictionary cloud sync, installed-assistant discovery, pairs beyond He<->En.
architecture-core.diagram: specs/001-layout-autocorrect/workshop/architecture-core.md — console-ASCII process topology + pipeline keeper diagram

agenda: Which components exist, on which IDesign layer, with what one-line responsibility?
May engines call accessors, or stay pure with data handed in by managers?
What are the extension mechanisms for language pairs, detection tiers, and AI providers?
Does the seamless-correction flow (including the race case) hold across the map?
component-design.decision: Agreed 16-component strict-IDesign map: Clients TrayClient + OverlayClient; Managers CorrectionManager (typing flow, correction transaction, privacy lifecycle) + SettingsManager (configuration, BYOK, exclusions); Engines WordAssemblyEngine, TranscriptEngine, MappingEngine, DetectionEngine (callback-only, hold the state); Accessors Keystroke, Focus, InputInjection, Layout, Dictionary, Llm, Audio, Settings. Engines are pure — no accessor calls, managers hand data in (stricter than classic IDesign, agreed deliberately; zero-mock unit tests). Extension: new language pair is data only (key map + dictionary); new tiers/providers are DI registrations. The seamless-correction flow including the trailing-remap race case was walked and agreed.
component-design.diagram: specs/001-layout-autocorrect/workshop/component-design.md — console-ASCII layered component map + agreed correction flow

agenda: Which quality attributes are design drivers, in what priority order?
What are the measurable thresholds for correction safety, latency, reliability, footprint, compatibility?
What must the system refuse to do?
requirements-nfr.decision: Agreed priority order: 1 correction safety (false-correction <1/1000, undo rate <2%, missed corrections are lesser defects), 2 felt latency (hook callback <1ms p99 allocation-free; dictionary verdict <10ms; dictionary correction transaction <50ms p95; LLM 500ms target with 2s hard timeout degrading to detection-only sound), 3 privacy (owned by security lens), 4 reliability (hook auto-recovery within 2s; crash never loses typed text or half-applies a correction), 5 resource footprint (idle ~0% CPU event-driven, <1ms passthrough, <150MB working set), 6 compatibility (mainstream edit surfaces; per-app exclusion as the valve). Refusals: no correction in password fields or excluded apps, no keystroke persistence, max one sentence to cloud LLM, no correction below the user-chosen conservatism level. False-correction numbers assumed until dogfood; slow-app acceptance case required. Amendment carried to component-design: IoC container composition, per-component interfaces, singleton lifetimes, mock-based tests.

agenda: How does the correction bubble behave and where is it positioned?
What is the sound design across correction / notify-only / AI-tier?
What is the undo mechanism, and does it conflict with the host app's Ctrl+Z?
What does the settings surface contain and where does it live?
Which accessibility, RTL and theming constraints are binding?
ui-ux.decision: Agreed the Crew-proposed visual design (no Figma/sketch exists; human explicitly delegated the visuals and confirmed the rendered layouts). Click-through caret-anchored bubble showing typed->corrected text plus the new layout, auto-fading ~1.2s, suppressible. Tray menu with status dot, pause, Correct/Notify-only mode, one-click exclusion of the foreground app, settings, quit. Three distinct sounds (correction / notify-only detection / AI-tier), individually mutable. Undo resolved after the human raised the Ctrl+Z conflict: Ctrl+Z rejected (swallowing breaks host-app undo; not swallowing gives unreliable host-granularity undo). Agreed a FLIP hotkey instead - double-tap Ctrl by default, Ctrl+Alt+Z configurable alternative, user-changeable; armed ~5s after a correction while it is still the most recent edit; flipping back marks the word do-not-correct for the session; corrections injected as a single burst so host Ctrl+Z remains a decent fallback. Settings window opened from tray (not resident). RTL correctness, light/dark themes, reduce-motion honored, sound as a non-visual parallel channel.
ui-ux.diagram: specs/001-layout-autocorrect/workshop/ui-ux.md — console-ASCII correction bubble + tray menu layouts

agenda: What must persist, what is memory-only, and what is never written at all?
Which storage technology: files with an in-memory trie, or SQLite?
Which component owns each data type?
How do schema changes and app updates avoid clobbering user data?
How are learned/never-correct words made inspectable?
data-storage.decision: Agreed three-tier data model. ON DISK per-user under %LOCALAPPDATA%\KeyContextAI: KeyMap files per layout pair (shipped, read-only, scancode -> char_a/char_b), Dictionary files per language (shipped plus user-extended: words with frequency, user_added, never_correct), and a single JSON Settings file (active pairs, mode, conservatism, sounds, bubble, excluded apps, hotkey, ai_provider) whose ai_credentials field is a DPAPI-encrypted blob. IN MEMORY ONLY: the transcript journal (keystrokes/words, layout provenance, correction status, epochs) and the session never-correct set, wiped on focus change, password field, pause and exit. NEVER WRITTEN: raw keystroke logs, per-correction history, window titles, password-field content, LLM request/response bodies. Storage technology is plain files plus an in-memory trie; SQLite rejected deliberately (dependency, schema and migrations for non-relational data) with the recorded flip trigger being dictionaries too large for memory. Ownership: DictionaryAccessor owns key maps and dictionaries, SettingsAccessor owns settings and credentials, TranscriptEngine owns in-memory typing state, no cross-reading. Every file carries schema_version and unknown versions are rejected loudly; user-added words live in a separate file from the shipped dictionary so updates never clobber them (and the deferred cloud sync becomes one-file sync). Flipped-back words land in the user's plain-text never_correct list, inspectable and editable as a trust feature.
data-storage.diagram: specs/001-layout-autocorrect/workshop/data-storage.md — console-ASCII data ownership and lifetime map (on-disk / in-memory / never-written)

agenda: Where are the trust boundaries and what is the attack surface?
How is the password-field gate enforced when detection is uncertain?
What prevents injected text landing in the wrong window?
How are BYOK credentials protected at rest?
What leaves the machine for the AI tier, and what counts as opt-in?
How is the supply chain and the malware-resemblance problem handled?
security-compliance.decision: Agreed three trust boundaries with controls. Boundary 1 capture: password gate is fail-closed (uncertain detection suspends capture), the process runs unelevated so elevated windows are invisible by design, and the transcript wipes on every focus change so text never crosses apps. Boundary 1 injection: correction is injected only into the window that produced the keystrokes; if focus changed between detection and injection the correction is abandoned, treated as a security control. Boundary 2 disk: DPAPI CurrentUser scope for API keys so another local account cannot decrypt them; no keystrokes, correction history or window titles on disk ever. Boundary 3 network: AI tier opt-in and off by default, one sentence of context with no user identifier, app name or window title, TLS only, local models close the boundary entirely. Human-sharpened opt-in rule: the opt-in is either the user configuring a provider/key OR the user answering yes when we detect an installed Claude/Copilot CLI or desktop app and ASK — detection alone never activates anything, and silent reuse of an unpointed credential is forbidden; a one-time confirmation before the first cloud call states exactly what is sent. Supply chain: minimal pinned dependencies, reproducible builds from public CI so the published binary matches public source, SECURITY.md plus a plain-language what-this-can-and-cannot-see README section.

agenda: What is the integration style and who owns the contract?
What request/response shape does the LLM tier use?
Which providers ship in MVP?
Can an installed Copilot/Claude CLI be used without an API key, and in .NET?
What are the timeout, retry and circuit-breaker semantics?
How are late/superseded responses handled?
How is provider compatibility tested?
integration-api.decision: Researched and agreed after the human challenged the first draft. Verified: MAF 1.0 GA 2026-04-03 with first-party connectors (Foundry, Azure OpenAI, OpenAI, Anthropic Claude, Bedrock, Gemini, Ollama); the GitHub Copilot agent type IS .NET-available (Microsoft.Agents.AI.GitHub.Copilot, CopilotClient.AsAIAgent) running on an authenticated Copilot CLI with NO API key; the Claude Agent SDK agent type (ClaudeAgent, prerequisite installed Claude Code CLI, no API key) exists but is Python-only and prerelease, while the Anthropic model provider (API key) is .NET-available. Decisions: direct in-process MAF call behind our ILlmAccessor contract, no self-hosted HTTP; structured request (typed text, one-sentence context, both layouts, dictionary candidate) and structured response (verdict correct|leave, text, confidence, tier, elapsed_ms) with no prose parsing; MVP providers are Azure OpenAI/Foundry, OpenAI, Anthropic Claude by key, and a local Ollama/OpenAI-compatible endpoint; MVP ships the Copilot-CLI zero-key discovery path (detect, ask, use) while the Claude Code CLI route is a recorded watch item that becomes configuration behind the same contract once it reaches .NET; 2s hard timeout returning verdict leave, Polly retry only on transient/429 with jitter under the budget, circuit breaker degrading to dictionary-only with an amber tray icon; every request carries a correction-transaction id and superseded late responses are discarded rather than applied; a fake plus one recorded-response integration test per provider guards MAF/provider drift. Flags recorded: hold one long-lived CLI-harness client (per-correction startup blows the 500ms budget) and supply no permission handler so the deny-all default keeps the agent away from shell/file/URL tools.

agenda: What does the user see for each failure mode?
What may a local diagnostic log contain, and may a verbose mode include text?
Is there any telemetry, and if so what is the payload, transport and consent model?
What recovery patterns apply to the hook, the AI tier and correction transactions?
observability-resilience.decision: Tray icon (green/amber/red with hover reason) is the primary observability surface. Local diagnostic log off by default, built as an in-memory ring buffer flushed only during quiet periods (~2s without a keystroke) so file I/O never competes with the correction hot path - the human's design; losing a log tail on crash is the accepted sacrifice. Standard log mode records events and outcomes with no text; a human-approved verbose bug-report mode is explicitly opt-in, session-scoped and self-deleting and MAY include text. The log doubles as the maintainer's research instrument for performance, correctness, memory, LLM invocation rate, double-correction count and correction quality as a function of typing speed. Session counters visible in settings validate the false-correction target during dogfood. Telemetry: the Crew's no-telemetry-ever proposal was replaced by the human with two separately-toggleable opt-in channels, both off by default - a session ping (random resettable install_id, version, os, active pairs, ai_tier; never username, machine name, app names or text) and an aggregate diagnostics channel (p50/p95 latency, LLM timeout rate, injection-abandon rate, hook restarts). Transport is a single HTTPS POST to an Azure Function with Application Insights behind it; IoT Hub and MQTT/Event Grid were considered and rejected as device-fleet machinery that would add a device-registration concept to a privacy-sensitive tool. Binding privacy rules: the endpoint must not log or retain IP addresses, and consent is a first-run explicit ask showing the exact JSON payload. The telemetry backend is post-MVP; v1 ships the client plumbing and consent UI with the switches present and off. Recovery: 2s hook watchdog with re-registration, Polly circuit breaker with half-open recovery for the AI tier, atomic correction transactions so mid-flight failure leaves text unchanged.
observability-resilience.diagram: specs/001-layout-autocorrect/workshop/observability-resilience.md — console-ASCII failure-mode map with user-visible outcomes

agenda: What is the hosting and packaging model for an OSS Windows desktop tool?
Which zero-budget code-signing path is actually available, and can Azure credits fund it?
Which CI lane belongs to this project's forge, and what runs in it?
What is the update model?
What repository governance and review gate apply?
devops-operations.decision: Local desktop tool, nothing server-side in MVP. Packaging: self-contained win-x64 and win-arm64, MSIX installer plus portable zip, winget manifest as the headline install path. Signing researched during the lens: primary path is Azure Artifact Signing (formerly Trusted Signing) at about $9.99/month Basic, payable from the human's Azure MVP credits, giving real Public Trust Authenticode with auto-renewing HSM-backed certs and a native GitHub Actions task - with the eligibility catch that individual developers must be US/Canada while organizations in Israel ARE supported, so validation runs under the human's named Israeli company entity ZioNet; fallbacks are the SignPath OSS program, Microsoft Store submission, and an unsigned zip with published SHA-256. CI is GitHub Actions matching the project's own forge: PR lane runs build, unit tests, the IDesign architecture test, markdownlint and Specrew governance validation; the tag release lane builds both architectures, packages MSIX and zip, signs, hashes and publishes a GitHub Release with reproducible-build flags honoring the security lens's binary-to-source promise. Update model (human decision): MSIX updates are produced by the CI release script when a new release is cut, never on a background timer. Governance: protect main (no direct commits, PR plus green required status checks, no force-push or deletion), required human approvals 0 for the solo maintainer but required status checks on, and Copilot automated PR review ENABLED as an advisory reviewer since the human has the subscription. The stale release_model local-only in .specrew/repository-governance.yml is corrected to a GitHub-based published-artifact model. Applying branch protection is an action pending the human's explicit go-ahead, not an open design question.

agenda: Is there an existing coding guideline or example project to emulate?
Which baseline craft defaults should be off?
Concurrency posture, error-handling style, and testing posture?
Which .NET/C# version posture and polymorphism mechanism?
Is the correction engine a reusable package or app-internal?
Which dependencies are earned, and which UI framework?
Which continuous co-review host reviews the implementation?
code-implementation.decision: No existing coding guideline or example project, so Specrew defaults apply (read from the human's agree-with-the-default reply and surfaced back to them as a filled gap). All baseline craft rules on with no exceptions requested. Forks agreed as presented: Channels pipeline with the correction executor as a single consumer loop serialized by construction rather than explicit locking; exceptions only for exceptional cases with Result-style returns for expected failures (LLM unavailable, injection refused, detection inconclusive); test-first for the pure engines, test-after for the Win32 accessors, plus a mandatory CI architecture test enforcing the IDesign call rules; .NET 10 LTS with LangVersion latest, nullable on, warnings-as-errors, file-scoped namespaces and records for messages; interfaces plus DI with the Strategy pattern for detection tiers instead of conditional chains. Engine packaging recorded as app-internal library with clean seams and NuGet extraction deferred - a Crew-proposed default for the one fork with no stated lean, surfaced to the human. Dependency stance is earned-dependencies-only with MAF 1.0, Microsoft.Agents.AI.GitHub.Copilot, Polly 8, Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection plus Hosting, and WPF chosen over WinUI 3 for the tray-plus-overlay shape. Reviewer: the host list was run and presented verbatim (codex marked default at rank 85, then copilot 80, cursor-agent 70, antigravity 65, plus claude as the non-independent code-writer); the human selected COPILOT, explicitly overriding the default because their codex tokens are exhausted, and the choice was persisted with specrew review --host copilot --authorization-ref workshop-001-layout-autocorrect.
